chapter_theme: Twenty verses of four gems each, many defining a common word anew (stranger, mother, the sweet eater) or naming what thrives, withers, burns or dies before an unfit receiver, ranging from the king's army to household giving, karma and the constant order of the world.

41.reading: All lives, at birth, do not leave though told to go and, at death, do not stay though told to stay; wealth swells of itself when the good lady consents, and when ruin comes even what was in plain sight vanishes.
41.nuance: The first two gems are one sentence about உயிரெனைத்தும், split by birth and death; the third gives no subject for what grows, and நல்லாள் is most likely Fortune (Tiru), so the swelling is of wealth. The four together set coming and going, gain and loss, beyond anyone's command.

items.claim: at birth a life does not depart though told to go
at death a life does not stay though told to stay
when the good lady (Fortune) consents, it grows of itself
in the time of ruin even what was seen vanishes from sight

42.reading: The glory of fighters withers without war, every tree withers without roots that go down, the tall neytal withers without a sluice to bring water, and the glory of kings withers away without an army.
42.nuance: Two natural images sit between two martial ones, so the army is set down as the root and the water-channel of a king's glory rather than its ornament.

items.claim: the glory of fighting men withers when there is no war
every tree withers without roots that strike down
the tall neytal withers without a sluice through which water flows
the glory of kings withers without an army

43.reading: Those called strangers are those without good nature, those called dear to everyone are the worthy, the excellent one called father is one's teacher, and the one called mother is the deed one did before.
43.nuance: Each gem redefines a kinship word: stranger and beloved by character, father as the teacher, and mother as one's own former deed, the source from which one's present life is born. The last turns the household's closest word into a word for karma.

items.claim: those called strangers are the people without good nature
those called beloved of all are the worthy
the excellent father is one's own teacher
the mother is the deed one did earlier

44.reading: Fortune perishes the moment shame is lost, action is ruined of itself by the five once they have taken their course, the green crop's unfailing goodness perishes without water, and the friendship of friends perishes when the good they gain changes.
44.nuance: ஐவர் 'the five' is read here as the five senses running their own way; the line gives no noun, and பொறி on line 1 can mean the senses as well as fortune. The fourth gem treats friendship's end on lost advantage as a natural fact, like a crop without water, rather than as a vice.

items.claim: fortune is lost the moment shame is lost
action is ruined by the five once they run their own course
the unfailing goodness of green crop perishes without water
friends' friendship perishes when the benefit changes

45.reading: A kindness dies before those who do not know kindness, a guest who has come dies before those without welcome, a song of rare composition dies before those who do not know melody, and a lover's sulk dies in the heart of one who does not understand sulking.
45.nuance: All four are offerings that live only in a receiver able to take them: gratitude, hospitality, art and love fail not through the giver but through the one before whom they are set.

items.claim: a good deed dies before those who do not know good
a guest who arrives dies before those who have no desire to receive him
a song of rare composition dies before those who do not know melody
a sulk dies in the heart of one who does not understand sulking

46.reading: Scent tells that a flower is there, spoken words tell, when weighed, the quality of a person's doing, the mind tells the evil packed within, and nothing tells the intention beforehand as the face does.
46.nuance: The four are signs and what they disclose; the last is a ranking, since nothing discloses earlier (முன்) than the face, and the face outruns even the mind of line 3.

items.claim: the presence of a flower is told by its scent
the worth of one's doing is told by one's words when they are weighed
evil packed inside is told by the mind
the intention is told first by the face, and nothing tells it sooner

47.reading: The people of the great earth have nothing without rain, there is no rain where there are no ascetics, no penance where there is no king, and no king where there are no householders.
47.nuance: The gems form a chain, each resting on the next, so the whole order of world, rain, penance and kingship rests at last on the householder.

items.claim: the people of the earth have nothing without rain
rain does not fall where there are no ascetics
penance does not exist where there is no king
a king does not exist where there are no householders

48.reading: A cool woven garland flourishes by its flowers, the bees all flourish by pollen, people flourish by faultless deeds, and honey flourishes by its own buds.
48.nuance: கரும்பு is read as the bee, which suits தாது (pollen), not as sugarcane; நறா may be honey or toddy. Three things of the flower frame one human one, so a person's deeds are to him what blossom is to garland and honey.

items.claim: a cool woven garland thrives by its blossoms
the bees all thrive by pollen
people thrive by faultless deeds
honey thrives by its own buds

49.reading: Anger is at all times hard for the eminent, living apart from one's companions is hard for those born into a family, sharing out food is hard for those who hold back, and saying 'there is nothing' to those who beg is hard for anyone.
49.nuance: Three gems tie a difficulty to a kind of person; the fourth widens it to everyone, so refusing a beggar is set as harder than the others. வரைந்தார் is read as those who set limits on giving.

items.claim: hostility is always hard for the eminent
living after leaving one's companions is hard for those born into kin
sharing out food is hard for those who hold back
saying 'nothing' to those who beg is hard for anyone

50.reading: Food burns when it enters a body that takes no pleasure in it, speech burns those without brightness of mind, a man's former deed, which knows no bound, burns him, and even a king is burned by the army that has joined him.
50.nuance: Each thing meant to sustain or serve turns on its holder: food, words, one's own past acts and one's own army. The last carries the theme to the king.

items.claim: food burns a body that takes no pleasure in it
speech burns those without brightness of mind
a man's former deed burns him without limit
the army that has joined him burns even a king

51.reading: Scorning a person is itself a thing to be scorned, words of counsel are things to be pondered, the path of dharma is a thing to join after knowing it within, and the meanings of the many books are things to be examined.
51.nuance: Each gem gives the right act toward a thing (to deride, to ponder, to join, to sift), and the first turns back on the scorner: contempt is matter for contempt.

items.claim: scorning a man is a thing for derision
words of counsel are things to be pondered
the path of dharma is to be joined after knowing it within
the meaning of the many books is to be examined

52.reading: There are tanks that hold rivers within them, there are subjects whom glorious kings desire, there are songs that reach the ancient Veda, and there are acts of beneficence equal to sacrifice.
52.nuance: Each gem says a lesser thing can equal a greater: a tank a river, a subject the king's desire, a song the Veda, giving a sacrifice. வேளாண்மை is read as beneficence, as in the Kural, though it can also mean husbandry.

items.claim: there are tanks that contain rivers
there are subjects that glorious kings desire
there are songs that attain to the ancient Veda
there is beneficence equal to sacrifice

53.reading: The verse says the vellalan is the one who owns oxen, the brahmin the one who does not accept, the cock the one that wins with a single strike, the woman of household life one who has wisdom with her beauty, and the commander the one who holds his army close.
53.domain_note: defines the marks of birth-groups and roles
53.nuance: The verse counts five, not four. வேளாளன் and பார்ப்பான் are birth-group names, and the verse defines each by a mark (oxen; not accepting), which can be read as naming what each group should have or as limiting the name to those who have it. ஏலாதான் is read as one who does not accept gifts; it may mean one who does not take up some work.

items.claim: the vellalan is the man who owns oxen
the brahmin is one who does not accept
the cock is what wins with one strike
the woman of household life is one with wisdom as well as beauty
the commander is the one who holds his army close

norm.note: defines birth-group names (vellalan, brahmin) and the wife by the marks the period expected of them

54.reading: Kings who own elephants delight in their fury and love to ride swift horses, good men delight in the modesty of good women with curved earrings, and the bad delighting in the bad is ruin.
54.nuance: Three delights are named as fitting to their owners, and the fourth turns the pattern: when like delights in like among the bad, the delight is ruin.

items.claim: kings who own elephants delight in their fury
kings love to ride swift horses
good men delight in the modesty of good women
the bad delighting in the bad is ruin

55.reading: No organ excels the eye, no kin is closer than the husband, no wealth is brighter or fuller than children, and no god is to be counted with the mother who bore one.
55.nuance: Four superlatives each name the first of its kind; the second speaks from a wife's place (கொண்டான், the man who took her) and the fourth sets the mother above any god.

items.claim: no bodily organ is better than the eye
no kin is closer than the husband
no wealth is brighter or fuller than children
no god can be counted alongside the mother who bore one

norm.note: ranks the husband as a wife's closest kin, a household norm of the period

56.reading: Those who love the learned are like the learned, those without kindly regard and those who join enemies are like enemies, and the small-minded who do not plainly say what has befallen them are like an anthill where a snake lives hidden.
56.nuance: The grouping of lines 1 and 2 is unclear: கண்ணோடார் may stand alone or with செற்றாரைச் சேர்ந்தவர். The verse judges people by what they cling to and by what they conceal.

items.claim: those who love the learned are like the learned
those without kindly regard are like enemies
those who join enemies are like enemies
the small-minded who hide what befell them are like an anthill hiding a snake

57.reading: The excellent gain excellent deeds, those who are not wanted gain unwanted deeds too, those who delight in dharma are born again everywhere, and those who renounce belong to heaven.
57.nuance: Line 3 is hard to divide: பிறப்பார் is doubled, and அறனின் புறுவர் can be read as those who rejoice in dharma. On the reading taken here it sets household dharma, which leads to rebirth, against renunciation, which leads to heaven.

items.claim: the excellent gain excellent deeds
the unwanted gain unwanted deeds as well
those who delight in dharma are born again
those who renounce are of heaven

58.reading: The days and the two lights exist always, disease and labour are always alike, givers and takers are always the same, and those born and those who die always exist.
58.nuance: Where most verses on this theme stress that the person passes, this one stresses that the pattern stays: sun and moon, sickness and work, giving and taking, birth and death are permanent features of the world.

items.claim: the days and the two lights always exist
disease and labour are always alike present
givers and takers are always the same
those born and those dying always exist

59.reading: The one who eats sweetly is the one who eats without killing life, the one fit to be shunned is the one who lives with a turned-away face, the one called lonely is he who has done no good, and the one called pleasant is he whose conduct no one resents.
59.nuance: Each gem redefines a common word by conduct: sweet eating by not killing, loneliness by having done no good. The verse runs to five lines where the others have four.

items.claim: the one who eats sweetly is he who eats without killing
the one fit to be resented is he who lives without a kind face
the lonely one is he who has done no good
the pleasant one is he whose conduct no one resents

norm.note: names eating without killing as the sweet way of eating, a diet rule of non-killing

60.reading: The one who eats after giving is the one who plants fame, the one who eats from another's hand is called a kaangi, going before those who are not one's own becomes plainly laughable, and begging from one who does not know one's plight becomes enmity.
60.nuance: காங்கி is a rare word; it plainly names the dependant who lives from another's hand. The first two gems set giver against taker, the last two count the costs of asking.

items.claim: the one who eats after giving plants fame
the one who eats from another's hand is called a kaangi
going before those not close to one becomes a laughing-stock
begging from one who does not know one's plight turns to enmity

links.note: Kural 376 says what is one's lot will not stay though guarded nor go though thrown away; the verse says the same of life itself at birth and at death.
links.teaches: The couplet's law of lot, said of possessions, is extended to the life that holds them: being born and dying are the first goods one cannot keep or refuse.
links.list_adds: It sets life's coming and going beside Fortune's swelling and ruin's vanishing, so birth, death, gain and loss become one set of things outside command.

links.note: Kural 761 ranks a complete, wound-fearing army first among a king's wealth; the verse says a king's glory withers without one.
links.teaches: Read together, the army is both the king's chief possession and the root his fame grows from, so losing it is not a loss of goods but a drying-up of renown.
links.list_adds: It puts the king's army in a row with war for warriors, roots for trees and the sluice for the neytal, so the army becomes the hidden supply of glory, not a holding.

links.note: Naladiyar 101 pictures an old deed seeking out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the verse calls one's former deed one's mother.
links.teaches: The two images run the bond in opposite directions: in the Naladiyar the deed hunts the doer like a calf its mother, here the deed is the mother who bore the doer.
links.list_adds: It ends a list that redefines stranger, beloved and father, so karma takes the place of the mother in a whole remade family.

links.note: Kural 812 dismisses the friendship of misfits who come with gain and leave without it; the verse says friends' friendship perishes when the good changes.
links.teaches: The couplet blames a bad kind of friend, while the verse makes the fading of friendship with advantage a natural law, like a crop without water, so the fault may lie in friendship itself.
links.list_adds: It sets friendship's decay beside a crop dying without water, so the end of interested friendship reads as nature, not as a vice of some.

links.note: Kural 1019 says lasting shamelessness burns every good; the verse says fortune perishes the moment shame is lost.
links.teaches: The verse makes the couplet's slow burning instant (போழ்தே, the very moment), so the loss of shame is shown as a sudden rather than gradual ruin.
links.list_adds: It puts the loss of shame first in a list of four ruins of the same form, so shame stands with water for crops as the thing whose absence ends goods at once.

links.note: Kural 1308 asks what use suffering is where there is no lover to know it; the verse says a sulk dies in one who does not understand sulking.
links.teaches: Both put the life of oodal in the partner's understanding, and the verse adds that the same is true of gratitude, guests and song, so the lover's plight is one case of a general rule.
links.list_adds: It sets the sulk beside a kindness, a guest and a song, so love's quarrel becomes one of four gifts that die in an incompetent receiver.

links.note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; the verse says a guest dies before those without the wish to receive.
links.teaches: The couplet locates the guest's wilting in a visible face, the verse in the host's absent desire, so the face is shown as the sign of a want of welcome that kills even before it shows.
links.list_adds: It sets the guest beside gratitude, song and sulk, so hospitality is a gift that needs a fit receiver, like art.

links.note: Kural 707 asks whether anything is as knowing as the face, which reaches first in joy or anger; the verse says nothing tells the intention beforehand as the face does.
links.teaches: Both make the face faster than speech, and the verse sets this speed against slower signs, scent, weighed words and the mind, so priority in time is what makes the face the best witness.
links.list_adds: It ranks the face above three other signs (scent, words, mind), making the couplet's claim a contest won rather than a lone assertion.

links.note: Kural 19 says giving and penance will not last if the sky does not give rain; the verse says rain does not fall where there are no ascetics.
links.teaches: The Kural makes penance depend on rain and the verse makes rain depend on penance, so together they describe a circle in which ascetic and sky sustain each other.
links.list_adds: It makes rain one link in a chain that ends with king and householder, so the couplet's dependence becomes a whole social order resting on the house.

links.note: Thirikadugam 96 names the knowing wife, the ascetic who keeps his vow and the good king as three at whose word rain falls; the verse makes rain rest on ascetics, ascetics on the king, the king on householders.
links.teaches: Both books make human virtue the cause of rain, but Thirikadugam sets three causes side by side while the verse lines them up, so one gives co-equal powers and the other a chain of dependence ending in the household.

links.note: Naladiyar 111 says saying 'I have none' of what one cannot give is no disgrace and is the way of the world; the verse says saying 'nothing' to beggars is hard for anyone.
links.teaches: The quatrain frees refusal from blame and the verse says it is still hard to say, so together they separate guilt from difficulty: refusal is no fault but costs everyone.
links.list_adds: It ranks refusal as the hardest of four hard things, the only one hard for anyone, whereas the quatrain only judges it.

links.note: Kural 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' and giving belong only to the well-born; the verse says saying 'nothing' to beggars is hard for anyone.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the refusal to refuse a mark of birth, the verse makes the reluctance to refuse universal, so lineage is no longer needed to explain it.
links.list_adds: It sets refusing beggars among difficulties tied to kinds of person (the eminent, the kin-born, the stingy) and frees this last one from any kind.

links.note: Kural 942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats after the last meal is digested; the verse says food burns a body that takes no pleasure in it.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the rule for eating, the verse the damage when the body cannot take food, so the pair shows food as medicine or fire depending on the body's state.
links.list_adds: It sets food beside words, past deeds and an army, all things meant to serve that turn and burn their holder.

links.note: Kural 423 says understanding is seeing the true substance of whatever is heard from whomever; the verse says the meanings of the many books are things to be examined.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the test for any utterance, and the verse applies it to the many books themselves, so even the written tradition must be sifted, not merely received.
links.list_adds: It puts sifting the books last in a sequence of right responses (deride contempt, ponder counsel, join dharma), so examination is the final act of a learner's conduct.

links.note: Kural 259 ranks not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices; the verse says there is beneficence equal to sacrifice.
links.teaches: Both measure an ethical act against sacrifice, but the Kural puts non-killing above it and the verse puts beneficence level with it, so sacrifice stays the standard in one and is outranked in the other.
links.list_adds: It makes beneficence equal to sacrifice as a tank can hold a river and a song reach the Veda, so the claim is one of a set of lesser things rising to the greater.

links.note: Thirikadugam 12 defines the vellalan as one who does not eat while a guest waits; the verse defines him as one who owns oxen.
links.teaches: Both define the same birth-group name by a mark, but one by hospitality and the other by owning the plough-ox, so the period's ethics offered rival tests, conduct or possession, for who deserved the name.

links.note: Kural 56 says she is a woman who guards herself, cares for her husband and keeps their good name without flagging; the verse says the woman of household life has wisdom with her beauty.
links.teaches: Both make பெண் a title to be earned, but the Kural earns it by guarding and serving while the verse asks for wisdom joined to beauty, a different test of the same name.
links.list_adds: It puts the wife among definitions of the farmer, the brahmin, the cock and the commander, so a woman's title is one of a set of role-names each tied to a mark.

links.note: Kural 460 says nothing brings more affliction than bad company; the verse says the bad delighting in the bad is ruin.
links.teaches: The couplet warns the good against bad company, the verse looks at the bad among themselves, so ruin comes not only from joining them but from the pleasure they take in each other.
links.list_adds: It closes a list of fitting delights (kings in elephants and horses, good men in modest women) with a delight that is ruin, so the last item undoes the pattern.

links.note: Kural 61 says nothing that can be gained matches children who come to know; the verse says no wealth is brighter or fuller than children.
links.teaches: The couplet's praise is conditional on the children's understanding while the verse gives it unqualified, and the verse places it among other firsts, so children are the first of wealth as the mother is first above the gods.
links.list_adds: It ranks children as one of four superlatives (eye among organs, husband among kin, mother above gods), so their worth is placed in a hierarchy of bests.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 30 counts a house where a snake lurks hidden as painful; the verse likens the small-minded who hide what has befallen them to an anthill where a snake dwells hidden.
links.teaches: The Innaa line names the hidden snake as a danger to live beside, and the verse turns it into a person, so the reader learns that the secretive man is that danger.

links.note: Kural 348 says those who wholly renounce reach the head and the rest are caught in the net; the verse says those who delight in dharma are born again and those who renounce are of heaven.
links.teaches: The couplet's net becomes in the verse rebirth earned by dharma itself, so even the righteous householder is among those still caught, while renunciation alone leaves.
links.list_adds: It sets renunciation after the rule that deeds follow their doers, so release is the end of a sequence on karma rather than a standalone praise.

links.note: Kural 336 says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is gone today; the verse says the born and the dying always exist.
links.teaches: The Kural looks at the individual who vanishes and the verse at the pattern that stays, so impermanence of persons is shown to sit within a permanence of kinds.
links.list_adds: It places birth and death beside the sun and moon, disease and labour, and givers and takers, all fixtures of the world, so mortality becomes one more constant.

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu 4 names not swelling one's flesh by eating flesh as foremost sweet; the verse says the one who eats sweetly is the one who eats without killing.
links.teaches: The two state one claim from two sides: Iniyavai calls the abstention sweet, and the verse calls the meal sweet only if it involves no killing, so sweetness belongs to the eating, not the food.

links.note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own can hold to grace; the verse redefines the sweet eater as one who eats without killing.
links.teaches: The couplet argues against flesh-eating from grace, the verse from the word 'sweet' itself, so the claim moves from the eater's heart to the meaning of a good meal.
links.list_adds: It sets the non-killing eater among redefinitions of the shunned, the lonely and the pleasant, so diet is judged by the same test of conduct as social standing.

links.note: Naladiyar 303 says the worthy go before no one except those who embrace them and say 'come in, eat'; the verse says begging from one who does not know one's plight becomes enmity.
links.teaches: The quatrain says whom the worthy may approach and the verse says what happens if they approach the wrong one: the request turns into enmity.
links.list_adds: It sets this cost beside the giver's fame, the taker's name and the laughter of going before strangers, so asking is weighed by its consequences on both sides.

source_issues: 43 line 1: the site's text lacks line 1 (flag site_diff); the line is kept here as the corpus gives it.
48 line 2: நந்துஞ் before கரும்பெல்லாந் has the wrong sandhi nasal; நந்துங் is expected.
53 lines 1-2: the semicolons are the editor's; the verse names five things where the work's form leads one to expect four.
57 line 3: the doubled பிறப்பார் and the division அறனின் புறுவர் leave the line hard to construe.
59: the verse has five lines where the other verses of the chapter have four.
